captions.F3: Figure 3.Enhancing anti-inflammatory pathways in microglia with engineered IL-10 cytokines(A) Schematic depicting the pro- and anti-inflammatory effects of wildtype (WT) IL-10 and engineered IL-10 variant (D25K, IL-10*) on myeloid cells and T cells.(B) Old male mice (25 months) were infused with vehicle control (n = 1), WT IL-10 (0.1 mg/mL and 0.02 mg/mL, n = 2, pooled) or engineered IL-10* (0.1 mg/mL and 0.02 mg/mL, n = 2, pooled). Young male mice (3 months, n = 2, pooled) were infused with vehicle control. Single-cell RNA-sequencing was performed as in Figure 2. Results with the higher concentration of IL-10 (0.1 mg/mL) are in Figure S4H–K. Figures 3, 4, S4B, S4C, and S4E are with the 0.02 mg/mL concentration.(C) UMAP clustering of all high-quality cells downsampled to 3,365 cells per condition, colored by cell-type.(D) Same as (C) colored by condition.(E-F) Log-normalized expression of IL-10 signaling genes Stat3 (E) and Tnf (F) in microglia of the SVZ. Horizontal lines: median.(G) Heatmap showing fold change in expression of genes in the IL-10 pathway in microglia. Red: upregulated, blue: downregulated genes with IL-10.(H-J) Primary microglia cells were stimulated with lipopolysaccharide (LPS, 0.1 μg/mL) with or without WT IL-10 or IL-10* (10mM) for 48 hours. Amounts of secreted IL-6 (I) and TNFα (J) cytokines were measured by ELISA. Data are mean ± s.e.m. (see Table S4 for independent repeat).(K) Log-normalized expression of Gzmb in T cells of the SVZ. Horizontal lines: median. Only T cells that expressed Gzmb were plotted.(L) Heatmap as in G but for T cells.(M) Each T cell was given a single score for each signature. Box plot displays the median and lower and upper quartile values. Permutation-based P-values, see Methods.P-values: two-sided Wilcoxon rank sum test unless otherwise specified. NS, not significant.See also Figure S4.
captions.F4: Figure 4.Net effect of engineered IL-10 cytokines on old microglia(A, B) MSigDB hallmark pathways enriched in the top 100 differentially up or down regulated genes in microglia from old mice treated with WT IL-10 (A) or IL-10* (B) versus old control. For all pathways shown, FDR < 0.05, EnrichR statistics.(C) Combined log-normalized expression of genes in the interferon-γ response pathway in microglia of the SVZ. Horizontal lines: median.(D) Heatmap showing fold change in interferon response genes in microglia. Red: upregulated, blue: downregulated with IL-10.(E) Inflammation scores for microglia in the SVZ of old control vs. young control, old WT IL-10 vs. old control and old IL-10* vs. old control mice.(F-H) Old male mice (24-25 months) were infused with vehicle control, WT IL-10 or engineered IL-10* for one week and FACS performed on microglia (CD45+CD11b+). FACS quantification and representative histograms of CD86 (G), BST2 (H), and MHC-I (H) MFI in freshly isolated microglia (n = 5-7 mice combined over two independent experiments, see Table S4). MFI values (~3,000 microglia cells) were normalized to those of the median of old control for each experiment.(I, J) Left: Representative immunofluorescence images of CD68 and IBA1 (I) or IFITM3 and TMEM119 (J) in SVZ brain sections. Red: IFITM3 (interferon response) or IBA1 (microglia); green: CD68 (activation marker) or TMEM119 (microglia); blue: DAPI. Scale bar: 20 μm. Right: quantification of mean CD68 or IFITM3 fluorescence intensity overlapping with microglia cell marker fluorescence (IBA1 or TMEM119) in SVZ sections from young control (4 months, n = 5), old control (n = 6), old WT IL-10 (n = 6) and old IL-10* (n = 4-5) treated male mice (24 months). Each dot represents one mouse (average of three coronal sections per mouse). One independent experiment.Data are mean ± s.e.m. P-values: two-sided Wilcoxon rank sum test. NS, not significant.See also Figure S4.
